name: Robot behind a PLC, over Modbus TCP (EXAMPLE: adapt to the site)
hint: the name of a program the PLC knows (upper case letters, digits and _); it must be on the device's list as NAME=<number>, the number the PLC program expects

steps.fail: the PLC says the robot is not accepting commands from outside ({reply})
the PLC says the robot's safety status is not OK ({reply})
the robot is not idle ({reply}: 0 idle, 1 running, 2 fault)
the PLC did not take the program number ({reply})
the PLC did not take the start ({reply})
the PLC did not take the start being released ({reply})
the PLC did not take the stop ({reply})

ready_when.why: it is not accepting commands from outside
its safety status is not OK

source: A register map INVENTED for PCHI's tests (docs/kuka.md and plcsim.rs), NOT any real PLC's or any robot's. Modbus TCP itself is a published standard and is implemented from it; what each address MEANS is the PLC programmer's, and how the PLC drives the robot (for a KUKA, its Automatic External inputs) is theirs and the robot programmer's.
notes: An EXAMPLE. It does nothing until the PLC programmer has written a program with this contract (or you have edited this file to match theirs) and every program number it can start has been validated by the robot's programmer. The reserved coils 30 to 39 stand for the machine's drives and fault acknowledgement: this profile promises never to write them, and the runtime refuses to load a profile that does. The start is a pulse: the number is written, the start coil is raised, then lowered, and if anything fails in between the start coil is lowered again. Not tested against any PLC or robot: only against a pretend PLC. A PCHI stop is a software request over a network, NOT an emergency stop.
